text: At any moment, a governance program has multiple issues open at once. An issue log is the single record of all of them — without one, "how are we actually doing" can only be answered by asking around.

An issue log tracks ID, description, domain, severity, status, and dates. Severity only matters if it changes behavior: critical gets same-day attention, high gets days not weeks, medium follows the normal backlog, low gets addressed when there's capacity. If critical and medium get the same response time, the label is decorative.

Escalation follows Chapter one's roles in order. Steward resolves what's within their domain. The data owner steps in when it crosses what the steward alone can decide. The governance committee handles cross-domain disputes. Sponsor or council is the last resort for organization-wide stakes.

An escalation path only works if it's used selectively. A program that pushes every minor issue to the sponsor trains the organization to ignore escalations — the real signal gets buried in noise. Escalation is for issues genuinely stuck at the current level, not a way to avoid owning a decision.
Next lesson closes the chapter: once an issue does land somewhere, who actually has the final say — decision rights.
